indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the word before it is only one possible arrangement of its letters, so another order is wanted

parts.note: the Moroccan port's name supplies all eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a balloon's helium was shipped out of Tangiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'perhaps' make Tangiers look like a guessed origin; it is simply the letters. Helium is the example, and the 'say' marks it as one member of a class.
explanation.definitionFit: Helium is one of the noble or inert gases, which barely react with anything, so it is a definition by example.

indicators.note: in a down entry 'up' means read from the bottom towards the top, which turns a word back to front

parts.note: jeans are made of denim

explanation.surface: Someone dug up a buried scrap of denim, as if at an archaeological site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dug ... up' reads as one phrasal verb, but 'up' belongs to the wordplay and 'Dug' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To mine is to dig out of the ground, so 'mined' is a plain synonym of the past tense 'dug'.

clue.text: Male graduate in an Asian city

parts.note: the first letter of the outer word AN

indicators.note: 'in' places the first pieces inside the word that follows, as something sits in a box

parts.note: an MA, a Master of Arts, is a graduate
M is the standard abbreviation for male
the second letter of AN, closing around M and MA

explanation.surface: A male graduate is living in some city in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an' looks like a plain article but it is the wrapper. Amman is the capital of Jordan, which sits in western Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: Amman, the capital of Jordan, is a city in the Middle East, which is geographically part of Asia.

clue.text: Painter lifts brace to bright light

indicators.note: in a down entry, to lift something is to send it upward, so the piece is read bottom to top

parts.note: a painter is an RA, a Royal Academician, and lifting it gives AR
a brace and a clamp both hold things firmly together

explanation.surface: A decorator hoists a support bracket up to fix a strong lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts, is the crossword's standard painter. 'lifts brace' reads as picking up a tool, but 'lifts' works only on the painter.
explanation.definitionFit: An arc lamp makes light from an electric spark jumping between electrodes, and is famously brilliant, used in searchlights and early cinema.

indicators.note: a tail is the end of something, so a tailless word has lost its final letter

parts.note: a plane is an aircraft
the tail of PLANE, its last letter, is removed

explanation.surface: An engineer studies the drawings for an aircraft with no tail fin.
explanation.walkthrough: A real tailless aircraft exists, which makes the surface convincing, but here the tail is just the last letter of PLANE.
explanation.definitionFit: A blueprint is a detailed design drawn up in advance, which is what a plan is.

indicators.note: the words 'hide' the answer by holding its letters inside them, across the gap between them

parts.note: the letters run from the end of 'Even' into 'nuisances'

explanation.surface: Even pests keep their tedium to themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' tempts you to take even letters, but it is simply where the hidden run begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is a French borrowing for weary, listless boredom, and English uses it as a straight synonym.

clue.text: So microphones not allowed for efficiency study

parts.note: ERGO is Latin for 'therefore', which is 'so'
NO is what you say when something is not allowed, as on a sign
MICS is the short form of microphones

explanation.surface: A time-and-motion expert bans microphones to make the office run better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So' is the Latin connective ergo, familiar from 'I think, therefore I am'. The answer takes 'not allowed' ahead of the microphones, the way a sign reads.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergonomics studies how people work with their tools and surroundings, aiming to make that work comfortable and efficient.

clue.text: Small ball over in chapel brambles

indicators.note: to turn something over is to flip it, so the hidden letters are read backwards
'in' says the letters are sitting inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run from the end of 'chapel' into 'brambles'

explanation.surface: A child's small ball has rolled into the brambles by the chapel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' here means flipped, not above, so the hidden letters are read from right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: A marble is a small glass ball used in children's games.

clue.text: It is annoying to worry a few

definitions.note: the whole phrase describes something that annoys; the answer is the adjective that phrase predicates

parts.note: to bother someone is to worry or trouble them
some means a few, an unspecified small number

explanation.surface: A grumble that it is irritating to fret over a handful of things.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the opening phrase: the answer describes whatever 'it' is, an annoying thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bothersome causes trouble or irritation, so it is annoying.

indicators.note: the two words cover the answer, holding its letters out of sight inside them

parts.note: the letters run from the end of 'Ranger' into 'berated'

explanation.surface: A park ranger is scolded for trampling over a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covering' pretends to be what the ranger did to the plant; it is the signal that the plant is concealed in the words before.
explanation.definitionFit: A gerbera is a daisy-like flowering plant from southern Africa, widely sold as a cut flower.

parts.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting before Easter
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: Someone is choosing between slow and fast time, and ends up with nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' pairs with 'Slow' as an opposite, but it means going without food, which points to Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: Lento is the Italian tempo marking in music for a slow pace.

definitions.meaning: to nag is to keep on at someone
a nag is a worn-out horse

explanation.surface: Someone is plagued by a stable of elderly horses.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses share the plural spelling, so the verb 'pesters' and the noun 'horses' land on the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: To nag is to pester with repeated complaint, and a nag is an old or poor-quality horse, so the plural covers both.

indicators.note: 'found in' says the answer can be found inside the next word

parts.note: the letters sit inside 'station'

explanation.surface: Cheap junk is on sale at a railway station.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden run sits inside a single word here, starting at its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tat is British slang for cheap, tasteless or poorly made goods.

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of the word, so its final letter goes

parts.note: a smirk is a smug, sneering smile
the last letter of the sneer word, dropped

explanation.surface: Someone very nearly sneers at a church that has got dirty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soil' looks like a noun for earth, but it is the verb, to dirty or stain.
explanation.definitionFit: To smirch is to make dirty or to sully a reputation, the same as to soil.

indicators.note: to go back is to go the wrong way, so the joined letters are read in reverse

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for Europe
America is the US

explanation.surface: Europe and America both support a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reads as 'support', but it is the instruction to reverse. Any short girl's name is fair game for 'girl' in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Sue is a girl's name, and crosswords use 'girl' to define any common female first name.

clue.text: Where, in France, birds going around are starving

indicators.note: 'in France' asks for the French word rather than the English one
something going around another thing encircles it, so the outer word wraps the inner

parts.note: ravens are birds, and RAVENS opens around the French word
OU is French for 'where'

explanation.surface: Somewhere in France, circling birds are desperately hungry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where, in France' reads as setting the scene, but it asks for the French word for 'where', OU.
explanation.definitionFit: Ravenous means extremely hungry, which is a plain synonym of starving.

parts.note: LA is French for 'the' (feminine)
a young seal is called a pup

explanation.surface: Someone happily takes on the French seal, as in an official stamp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seal' suggests a stamp, but it is the animal, and a baby one at that.
explanation.definitionFit: To lap up is literally to drink with the tongue, and figuratively to accept praise or news with eager delight.

clue.text: Play around in top frog's home

indicators.note: to play around is to mess about, so the letters are knocked out of their order
'in' places the rearranged letters inside the word that follows

parts.note: the letters of PLAY rearranged
a top is a LID, which opens around the other letters
the closing D of LID

explanation.surface: Someone fools about at the top of a frog's dwelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top' reads as an adjective, but it is the noun, a LID.
explanation.definitionFit: A lily pad is the floating leaf of a water lily, which cartoons and children's books make the frog's traditional perch.

indicators.note: correcting something means rearranging it, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A tennis coach says of a bad shot that they are fixing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'correcting' sounds like the coach fixing the bad shot, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A mishit is a shot in a ball game struck badly, so a faulty stroke.

parts.note: the indefinite article, a or an, gives A

indicators.note: short means the word is cut, losing its last letter

parts.note: very means extremely
the last letter of the word for extremely, dropped

explanation.surface: A terse phrase that reads like a description of a very small country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state' looks like a nation, but it is the verb, to declare.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to assert or declare something firmly, which is to state it.

clue.text: Hard to believe it's under small seat

indicators.note: in a down entry the piece under another is written below it, so it comes second

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small
a tall story is hard to believe, and 'it's' points back to that word

explanation.surface: Someone cannot believe there is something under a tiny seat.
explanation.walkthrough: TALL in the sense of 'a tall story' is an exaggerated one. A stall is a seat in a church choir or in the front of a theatre, the stalls.
explanation.definitionFit: A stall is a fixed seat, as in a choir stall, and the theatre stalls are the seats at ground level.

definitions.meaning: a plural noun for outings, holidays or excursions
a verb for catching a foot and losing balance

explanation.surface: Someone travels and keeps falling over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Journeys' is a noun and 'stumbles' a verb, and TRIPS serves as both.
explanation.definitionFit: A trip is a short journey, and to trip is to catch your foot and stumble, so the plural and the verb meet.

clue.text: Come fly without the Spanish — it's snug

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the named letters are taken out

parts.note: the letters to start from
EL is Spanish for 'the', and its E and L are removed

explanation.surface: An airline invitation promises a cosy flight, with no Spanish involved.
explanation.walkthrough: The E and L are not adjacent: remove the E from COME and the L from FLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Comfy is the informal, clipped form of comfortable, and snug means cosily comfortable.

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in your arms, so the outer word wraps around the letter

parts.note: to socialise is to MIX, which opens around the letter
N is the standard abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: Someone goes out to mingle and hug a naughty girl from the North.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Socialise' pretends to be the whole action, but it is MIX, the word that does the embracing.
explanation.definitionFit: A minx is a cheeky, impudent girl who makes mischief, usually said with some affection.

clue.text: City where Dorothy's dog seized boy

indicators.note: to seize something is to take hold of it, so the outer word grips the inner one

parts.note: Toto is Dorothy's dog in The Wizard of Oz, and TOTO opens around the boy
RON is a boy's name

explanation.surface: In the city where Dorothy's dog grabbed a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City where' sets up a news story, but the dog does the work. Toto from The Wizard of Oz is a favourite source of TOTO.
explanation.definitionFit: A bare 'City' defines any named city, and this one is the capital of Ontario and the largest in Canada.

clue.text: Visit cricket side before standing by

indicators.note: a piece that comes before another is written ahead of it, so the cricket side goes first

parts.note: the on side is the half of a cricket field on the batter's legs side
to call on someone is to visit them

explanation.surface: A cricket team pays a visit ahead of waiting in reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists 'Visit' first, but 'before' moves the cricket side ahead of it. In cricket the field is split into the on (or leg) side and the off side.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on call, like a doctor at night, is standing by ready to be summoned.

definitions.meaning: a verb, as a gardener cuts back branches
a noun, here a dried one from the breakfast table

explanation.surface: An instruction to slice some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut fruit' reads as one instruction, but it is a verb and a noun side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To prune is to cut back a plant or a budget, and a prune is a dried plum, so the word is both.
